2.2.1:
Why this matters

Six Sigma replaces opinions with data, and data has rules. The type of data you collect decides which charts and tests you can use later. Probability lets you reason about how likely things are. This topic is the vocabulary everything in Measure and Analyze is built on, so it is worth getting completely solid.

The big idea

Statistics answers two kinds of questions:

  1. Describing: what does our data look like? (descriptive statistics, 2.2.2)
  2. Inferring: what can a sample tell us about the whole process? (inferential statistics, Domain 3)

Before either, you need to know what kind of data you have and where it came from.

Continuous vs discrete data

Continuous data (also called variable data) is measured on a scale that can be divided as finely as your instrument allows: time (4.73 hours), weight (38,412 lb), temperature, distance, cost. Between any two values there is always another possible value.

Discrete data (also called attribute data) comes in separate, countable values or categories:

  • Counts: number of defects on an invoice (0, 1, 2…), number of late loads.
  • Pass/fail (binary): on time or late, damaged or not.
  • Categories: reason for delay (traffic, dock, paperwork), carrier name.

Why it matters: continuous data carries much more information. "Load arrived 3.5 hours late" tells you more than "late". Continuous data needs smaller samples and supports more powerful tools. When you can measure continuously, do.

Measurement scales

Data also differ in what you can do with the numbers. There are four scales, from least to most informative:

ScaleWhat it isExampleMeaningful operations
NominalNames or labels, no orderTerminal (Dallas, Memphis), defect typeCount, mode
OrdinalOrdered categories, but gaps not equalSatisfaction 1 to 5, FMEA ratings, small/medium/largeRank, median
IntervalEqual gaps, but zero is arbitraryTemperature in °F or °C, calendar datesAdd, subtract, mean
RatioEqual gaps and a true zeroWeight, time, distance, cost, countAll arithmetic, including "twice as much"

Nominal and ordinal are discrete. Interval and ratio are usually continuous. A memory aid: NOIR (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio).

Note that 80 °F is not "twice as hot" as 40 °F (interval scale, no true zero), but 80 lb is twice as heavy as 40 lb (ratio scale).

Population vs sample

  • A population is every item you care about: every load this carrier will ever haul under the current process. Its true values are parameters, written with Greek letters: μ (mu, population mean), σ (sigma, population standard deviation), N (population size).
  • A sample is the part of the population you actually measure: 50 loads from last month. Its values are statistics, written with Latin letters: x̄ (x-bar, sample mean), s (sample standard deviation), n (sample size).

We almost never know the true μ and σ. We estimate them from x̄ and s. Statistics (Domain 3) tells us how confident we can be in those estimates.

For a sample to represent the population, it should be random (every item had a fair chance of being chosen) and collected under the same conditions you want to learn about.

Probability basics

Probability is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) describing how likely an event is. If 8% of loads are late, P(late) = 0.08.

Complement rule. The probability something does not happen is 1 minus the probability it does:

P(not A) = 1 − P(A)

Addition rule (A or B). The probability that A or B (or both) happens:

P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)

You subtract P(A and B) because otherwise the overlap is counted twice. If A and B cannot happen together (mutually exclusive), P(A and B) = 0 and it simplifies to P(A) + P(B).

Multiplication rule (A and B). If A and B are independent (one happening does not change the chance of the other):

P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)

Conditional probability. The probability of A given that B has happened:

P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B)

Independent vs mutually exclusive

These are different ideas, and confusing them is a classic error:

  • Mutually exclusive: the events cannot both happen. A single load cannot be both "on time" and "late". Knowing one happened tells you the other did not.
  • Independent: one event does not affect the probability of the other. Whether today's load from Dallas is late has no effect on whether a load in Seattle is late.

Two events with non-zero probabilities that are mutually exclusive are never independent: if one happens, the other's probability drops to zero.

"At least one": use the complement

Questions often ask for the probability of at least one event. Calculate the chance of none and subtract from 1.

Each load has a 10% chance of being late, independently. In 3 loads, what is the chance at least one is late?

  • P(a load is on time) = 0.9.
  • P(all 3 on time) = 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.729.
  • P(at least one late) = 1 − 0.729 = 0.271.

Two counting distributions

Binomial: the number of "successes" (for example defectives) in n independent trials, each with the same probability p. Use it for pass/fail data.

P(x) = [n! ÷ (x!(n − x)!)] × pˣ × (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ˣ

5 invoices, each with a 10% chance of an error:

  • P(0 with errors) = 0.9⁵ = 0.590.
  • P(exactly 1) = 5 × 0.1 × 0.9⁴ = 5 × 0.1 × 0.6561 = 0.328.
  • P(at least 1) = 1 − 0.590 = 0.410.

Poisson: the number of events (for example defects) in a fixed amount of space or time, when they occur randomly at an average rate λ (lambda). Use it for defect counts.

P(x) = (λˣ × e^(−λ)) ÷ x!

Trucks average λ = 2 defects found at inspection:

  • P(0 defects) = e^(−2) = 0.135.
  • P(exactly 1) = 2 × e^(−2) = 0.271.
  • P(at least 1) = 1 − 0.135 = 0.865.

Rule of thumb: defectives (pass/fail units) → binomial; defects (counts per unit) → Poisson. (See 1.2.5 for defects vs defectives.)

Data collection plan

Before collecting data, write a plan so the data is useful and consistent:

  • What to measure (the Y and the suspect X's), with operational definitions.
  • How to measure it (instrument, method, form).
  • Who collects it (and are they trained?).
  • When and where: how often, which shifts, which locations.
  • How many: sample size.
  • Stratification factors: extra information recorded with each point (shift, terminal, driver, product), so the data can later be split to find patterns.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Pass/fail is discrete; measured length or time is continuous. Even if you record time to the nearest minute, it is continuous.
  • Independent is not mutually exclusive.
  • Sample symbols are Latin (x̄, s, n); population symbols are Greek (μ, σ, N).
  • "At least one" means 1 − P(none).
  • Ordinal ratings (1 to 5) do not have equal gaps, so averaging them is questionable.

Check yourself

  1. Classify as continuous or discrete: (a) seconds to answer a call, (b) whether a call was resolved, (c) number of errors on a form.
  2. Which scale is "customer satisfaction 1 to 5"?
  3. What symbol is the population standard deviation, and what is its sample counterpart?
  4. P(a pallet is damaged) = 0.02, independently. What is the probability that at least one of 10 pallets is damaged?
  5. Are "a load is late" and "a load is on time" independent, mutually exclusive, or both?
Show answers
  1. (a) Continuous, (b) discrete (pass/fail), (c) discrete (count).
  2. Ordinal.
  3. σ (population); s (sample).
  4. 1 − 0.98¹⁰ = 1 − 0.817 ≈ 0.183.
  5. Mutually exclusive (they cannot both happen), and therefore not independent.

Key takeaways

  • Continuous (measured) vs discrete (counted or categorized); continuous carries more information.
  • Scales: nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio (NOIR).
  • Population parameters (μ, σ, N) vs sample statistics (x̄, s, n).
  • Addition, multiplication (independent), conditional and complement rules; "at least one" = 1 − P(none).
  • Binomial for defectives, Poisson for defects.
  • Plan data collection: what, how, who, when, how many, stratification.
2.2.2:
Why this matters

A column of 200 numbers tells you nothing at a glance. Two or three well-chosen summary numbers, center and spread, tell you a lot. Almost every later calculation (capability, control limits, hypothesis tests) starts with a mean and a standard deviation.

The big idea

To describe data you need to know two things:

  1. Where is the middle? (central tendency)
  2. How spread out is it? (variation)

And, often, a third: what shape is it? (symmetric or skewed).

Measures of center

  • Mean (average): add all values and divide by how many. Symbol x̄ for a sample.
x̄ = Σx ÷ n

(Σ, capital sigma, means "add them all up".)

  • Median: the middle value when the data are sorted. With an even number of values, average the two middle ones.
  • Mode: the value that occurs most often.

Example, load times in hours: 4, 7, 6, 9, 4.

  • Mean = (4 + 7 + 6 + 9 + 4) ÷ 5 = 30 ÷ 5 = 6.
  • Sorted: 4, 4, 6, 7, 9. Median = 6.
  • Mode = 4.

The mean is pulled by extreme values; the median is not. If one load took 40 hours instead of 9, the mean jumps to 12.2, but the median stays 6. For skewed data, or data with outliers, the median is often a better description of a "typical" value.

Measures of spread

  • Range: largest minus smallest. Simple, but depends on only two points. For 4, 7, 6, 9, 4: range = 9 − 4 = 5.
  • Variance: the average squared distance from the mean.
  • Standard deviation: the square root of the variance, in the same units as the data. The most used measure of spread.
  • Interquartile range (IQR): Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle 50%. Resistant to outliers, like the median.

Calculating the sample standard deviation

s = √[ Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1) ]

Step by step for 4, 7, 6, 9, 4 (x̄ = 6):

xx − x̄(x − x̄)²

  1. Sum of squared deviations = 18.
  2. Divide by n − 1 = 4: variance s² = 4.5.
  3. Square root: s = √4.5 ≈ 2.12 hours.

Why n − 1? A sample's values are on average a little closer to their own mean than to the true population mean, so dividing by n would underestimate the spread. Dividing by n − 1 corrects this. For the whole population, divide by N: σ = √[Σ(x − μ)² ÷ N]. With the same five numbers treated as a population, σ = √(18 ÷ 5) ≈ 1.90.

Calculator trap: scientific calculators have two keys: σn (divides by n, population) and s or σn−1 (divides by n − 1, sample). For sample data, use the n − 1 key. You can convert: s = σn × √[n ÷ (n − 1)].

Shape and skew

Data piled symmetrically around the center (like the normal curve) have mean ≈ median ≈ mode. Many real processes are skewed:

A long right tail drags the mean toward it; the median sits between.

  • Right (positive) skew: a long tail to the right. Common for times (delivery times, repair times: they cannot go below zero but can run very long). Mean > median > mode.
  • Left (negative) skew: a long tail to the left. Mean < median < mode.

So if a question says "the mean is larger than the median", the data are skewed right.

Percentiles and quartiles

The p-th percentile is the value below which p% of the data fall. The quartiles split sorted data into four equal parts:

  • Q1 (25th percentile), Q2 (50th, the median), Q3 (75th).
  • IQR = Q3 − Q1.

"90% of deliveries arrive within 26 hours" means the 90th percentile of delivery time is 26 hours, which is often more meaningful to customers than the average.

Within vs overall variation

Data collected over time have two kinds of variation:

  • Within (short-term) variation: the variation inside small groups of consecutive measurements (subgroups), when conditions are nearly the same.
  • Overall (long-term) variation: the variation of all the data together, including shifts and drifts between subgroups.

Overall is always at least as large as within. The difference shows how much the process moves over time. This distinction drives Cp versus Pp in capability (2.4) and the 1.5σ idea in 1.1.1.

Variances add, standard deviations do not

When two independent sources of variation combine (for example, time to load plus time to drive), their variances add:

σ²(total) = σ²₁ + σ²₂

If loading time has σ = 3 minutes and transit time has σ = 4 minutes, the total has σ² = 9 + 16 = 25, so σ = 5 minutes, not 7. This is why measurement error and process variation combine the way they do in MSA (2.3).

Other formulas worth recognizing

  • Weighted mean: Σ(w × x) ÷ Σw. If 3 loads took 5 h and 1 load took 9 h, the weighted mean = (3 × 5 + 1 × 9) ÷ 4 = 6 h.
  • Mean of grouped data: Σ(f × class midpoint) ÷ n, used when data come in a frequency table.
  • Mean deviation: Σ|x − x̄| ÷ n, the average absolute distance from the mean (for 4, 7, 6, 9, 4: (2 + 1 + 0 + 3 + 2) ÷ 5 = 1.6).
  • Coefficient of variation: s ÷ x̄, spread relative to the mean, useful to compare processes with different averages (low exam yield).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Outliers pull the mean, not the median.
  • Mean > median means right skew.
  • Sample s divides by n − 1. Use the right calculator key.
  • Standard deviations do not add; variances do, for independent sources.

Check yourself

  1. Data: 2, 3, 3, 5, 12. Find the mean, median and mode.
  2. Which measure of center would you report for these data, and why?
  3. Compute s for 10, 12, 14.
  4. Two independent sources have σ = 6 and σ = 8. What is the combined σ?
  5. A delivery-time dataset has mean 31 hours and median 26 hours. Which way is it skewed?
Show answers
  1. Mean = 25 ÷ 5 = 5; median = 3; mode = 3.
  2. The median (3), because the outlier 12 pulls the mean up.
  3. Mean 12; deviations −2, 0, 2; squares sum to 8; s² = 8 ÷ 2 = 4; s = 2.
  4. √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10.
  5. Right (positive) skew, because the mean is above the median.

Key takeaways

  • Center: mean (pulled by outliers), median (resistant), mode.
  • Spread: range, variance, standard deviation, IQR.
  • s = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)]; population σ divides by N.
  • Right skew: mean > median > mode.
  • Within (short-term) vs overall (long-term) variation.
  • Independent variances add: σ_total = √(σ₁² + σ₂²).
2.2.3:
Why this matters

The normal distribution is the most important shape in statistics. Many processes produce roughly normal data, and many tools (capability indices, control limits, t-tests) assume it. You need to use it to calculate probabilities, and to check whether your data actually follow it.

The big idea

The normal distribution is the symmetric, bell-shaped curve. It is completely described by two numbers:

  • μ (mean): where the center is.
  • σ (standard deviation): how wide it is.

Change μ and the bell slides left or right. Change σ and it gets wider and flatter, or narrower and taller. The total area under the curve is 1 (100% of the data), and the area over any interval is the probability of a value falling there.

The empirical rule (68, 95, 99.7)

For any normal distribution:

The shares are the same for every normal distribution, whatever its mean and σ.

  • About 68% of values fall within ±1σ of the mean.
  • About 95% within ±2σ.
  • About 99.7% within ±3σ.

If delivery times are normal with mean 40 hours and σ = 4 hours, about 68% take 36 to 44 hours, 95% take 32 to 48 hours, and nearly all take 28 to 52 hours.

The z-score

To find the probability for any value, convert it to a z-score: how many standard deviations it is from the mean.

z = (x − μ) ÷ σ

Every normal distribution becomes the standard normal distribution (mean 0, σ 1) after this conversion, so one table works for all of them.

Using the z table

A standard normal table gives the area to the left of a z value (the probability of being below it).

The table gives the left area; the right tail is 1 minus it.

Example 1: above a value. Delivery times: μ = 40, σ = 4. What fraction take more than 46 hours?

  1. z = (46 − 40) ÷ 4 = 1.5.
  2. Table: area left of 1.5 = 0.9332.
  3. Above: 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668, about 6.7%.

Example 2: below a value. Fraction under 34 hours? z = (34 − 40) ÷ 4 = −1.5. By symmetry, area below −1.5 = 0.0668.

Example 3: between two values. Fraction between 36 and 48 hours?

  1. z for 36 = −1; z for 48 = +2.
  2. Area left of 2 = 0.9772; area left of −1 = 0.1587.
  3. Between: 0.9772 − 0.1587 = 0.8185, about 82%.

Example 4: symmetric interval. P(−z < Z < z) = 2 × (left area at z) − 1. For z = 1.96: 2 × 0.975 − 1 = 0.95.

A quirk of the IASSC reference document

The reference document (version 1.4.2) has two z tables. One lists negative z values (−4.9 to 0) and gives the left-tail area, as expected (z = −1.96 gives 0.02500). The second is titled "Right Tail Area" for z from 0 to 4.9, but its values are actually the area to the left (it shows 0.97500 at 1.96). So for P(Z > z), use 1 − (that table's value), or look up −z in the negative table. The table stops at 4.9 and prints tiny tails as 0.00000, so for 6σ-level questions use the known 3.4 DPMO rather than the table. Check this against your own copy, since versions differ.

Is my data normal? Normality tests

Many tools assume normal data, so you check. A normality test is a hypothesis test (Domain 3) with:

  • Null hypothesis (H₀): the data come from a normal distribution.
  • Alternative (H₁): they do not.

Common tests: Anderson-Darling (Minitab's default), Shapiro-Wilk, Ryan-Joiner, Kolmogorov-Smirnov. All produce a p-value:

  • p ≤ 0.05: strong evidence the data are not normal. Reject H₀. Memory aid: "if p is low, the null must go."
  • p > 0.05: not enough evidence to say the data are non-normal. You fail to reject H₀. This is not proof that the data are normal, just that the test found no strong evidence against it.

Sample size matters: with very few points (say 10), a test can almost never detect non-normality; with thousands, it flags tiny, unimportant departures. Always look at the picture too.

The normal probability plot

A probability plot plots each data point against where it would fall if the data were perfectly normal. If the data are normal, the points lie close to a straight line (within the curved confidence bands software draws). Curves, S-shapes and points peeling away at the ends show skew, heavy tails or outliers.

Why data are not normal

  • Skewed processes: times, counts and anything bounded at zero.
  • Mixed populations: two shifts, two machines or two suppliers combined (often bimodal, two humps).
  • Outliers: a few wild points from special causes or data errors.
  • Bounded data: values that cannot exceed a limit (100%, zero defects).
  • Coarse measurement: values rounded so much that only a few distinct values appear.

The fix depends on the cause: separate mixed populations (stratify), investigate outliers, use a transformation or a non-normal tool for naturally skewed data.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • p = 0.02 on a normality test means the data are not normal (p is low, reject normality).
  • p = 0.30 does not prove normality; it means no strong evidence against it.
  • Left-area tables: for "greater than", use 1 − table value.
  • ±1σ, ±2σ, ±3σ = 68%, 95%, 99.7%.

Check yourself

  1. What percentage of a normal distribution lies within ±2σ?
  2. μ = 100, σ = 10. What is the z-score of 85?
  3. For the same process, what fraction is above 120? (Area left of z = 2 is 0.9772.)
  4. An Anderson-Darling test gives p = 0.004. What do you conclude?
  5. A histogram shows two humps. What is the likely reason the data are not normal?
Show answers
  1. About 95%.
  2. z = (85 − 100) ÷ 10 = −1.5.
  3. z = 2; above = 1 − 0.9772 = 0.0228, about 2.3%.
  4. Reject normality: the data are not normal.
  5. Two populations mixed together (for example two shifts or machines).

Key takeaways

  • Normal curve: symmetric, defined by μ and σ.
  • 68% within ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ, 99.7% within ±3σ.
  • z = (x − μ) ÷ σ; tables give the left area; right tail = 1 − left.
  • Normality tests: H₀ = normal; p ≤ 0.05 means not normal; p > 0.05 is not proof of normality.
  • Check the probability plot; non-normality comes from skew, mixtures, outliers, bounds or coarse rounding.
2.2.4:
Why this matters

A good chart shows in seconds what a table hides for hours: patterns, shifts, outliers, clusters. Plot the data before calculating anything. The exam often describes a situation and asks which chart fits it.

The big idea

Every chart answers a different question. Match the chart to the question:

QuestionChart
What is the shape of one set of data?Histogram, dotplot, stem-and-leaf
How do several groups compare?Boxplot, individual value plot, interval plot
How does it behave over time?Run chart (and control charts, 5.2)
Are two continuous variables related?Scatterplot
Is it normal?Normal probability plot
Which categories matter most?Pareto chart

Histogram

A histogram groups data into ranges (bins) and draws a bar for how many values fall in each. It shows shape (symmetric, skewed, bimodal), center and spread.

  • Bin choice matters: too few bins hide the shape, too many make it jagged. Software defaults are usually reasonable.
  • Needs a fair amount of data (roughly 30 or more points, better 50 to 100) to show a reliable shape.

Two humps usually mean two different populations mixed together.

A bimodal (two-humped) histogram is a strong clue that two populations are mixed: two shifts, two machines, two suppliers. Split (stratify) the data and plot each group separately.

Boxplot

A boxplot (box-and-whisker plot) summarizes a distribution with five numbers and flags outliers:

The box holds the middle half of the data; the line inside is the median.

  • The box runs from Q1 to Q3 (the middle 50%, the IQR).
  • The line in the box is the median.
  • Whiskers extend to the furthest data points within 1.5 × IQR of the box.
  • Points beyond that are plotted individually as outliers.

Boxplots are excellent for comparing groups side by side: delivery times by terminal, cycle time by shift. You can instantly see which group has a higher median or more spread.

Other displays

  • Dotplot: one dot per value along a scale. Great for small data sets; shows every point.
  • Individual value plot: every data point plotted by group. Like a dotplot for comparing groups.
  • Interval plot: the mean of each group with a confidence interval bar (usually 95%). Used to compare group means; if intervals barely overlap, the means likely differ.
  • Stem-and-leaf plot: a text histogram that keeps the actual digits (stem = leading digits, leaves = last digit).

Run chart

A run chart plots data in time order with a center line at the median. It reveals behavior over time that a histogram hides:

  • Shift: a run of many consecutive points (commonly 6 or more, some texts use 8) all on one side of the median, suggesting the process level changed.
  • Trend: many consecutive points steadily rising or falling (commonly 5 to 7 or more).
  • Cycles: a repeating up-and-down pattern (weekly, daily, seasonal).
  • Oscillation, or too many runs: points zig-zagging up and down constantly, which can mean over-adjustment or mixed sources.
  • Too few runs: points stay on one side for long stretches, which suggests shifts.

Run charts need no statistical calculation beyond the median and work with little data, so they are useful early in a project. Control charts (5.2) add statistically calculated limits.

Scatterplot

A scatterplot plots pairs of continuous values: one variable on each axis. It shows whether they are related:

  • Points rising left to right: positive relationship (more miles, more fuel).
  • Falling: negative relationship (more experience, fewer errors).
  • A cloud with no pattern: no relationship.
  • A curve: a non-linear relationship.

It shows association, not proof of cause. The relationship is quantified with correlation and regression (3.3).

Normal probability plot and Pareto chart

Covered in 2.2.3 (probability plot, to judge normality) and 1.2.4 (Pareto, to rank categories).

Worked example

Which chart?

  1. "Compare loading times at our four terminals." Boxplot (or individual value plot).
  2. "Has our on-time rate changed since the new dispatch system went live?" Run chart (time order).
  3. "Does trailer age relate to repair cost?" Scatterplot.
  4. "What does the distribution of fuel use per trip look like?" Histogram.
  5. "Which reasons for claims matter most?" Pareto chart.
  6. "Are the cycle-time data normal?" Normal probability plot.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Comparing groups = boxplot (or interval/individual value plot).
  • Behavior over time = run chart. A histogram loses time order.
  • Two continuous variables = scatterplot.
  • Bimodal histogram = mixed populations, not a bad measurement.
  • A boxplot outlier is beyond 1.5 × IQR from the box, not beyond 3σ.

Check yourself

  1. What does the line inside a boxplot's box show?
  2. A team wants to see whether call volume varies by day of the week over three months. Which chart?
  3. Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 30. Beyond what values would points be plotted as outliers?
  4. What does a cloud of points with no pattern on a scatterplot suggest?
  5. On a run chart, 9 consecutive points are above the median. What does this suggest?
Show answers
  1. The median.
  2. A run chart (time order); cycles by day of week will show as a repeating pattern.
  3. IQR = 10; 1.5 × IQR = 15; outliers are below 20 − 15 = 5 or above 30 + 15 = 45.
  4. No relationship between the two variables.
  5. A shift: the process level has probably changed.

Key takeaways

  • Histogram: shape; bimodal means mixed populations.
  • Boxplot: median, Q1 to Q3 box, whiskers to 1.5 × IQR, outliers; best for comparing groups.
  • Run chart: time order; look for shifts, trends, cycles, oscillation.
  • Scatterplot: relationship between two continuous variables.
  • Pick the chart that answers the question.
